b: The hardest part of investing for me was learning how to save. Mrs Accumulator and I would spend all we had, though we knew deep down it would catch up with us in the end.
Restraining our spendaholic selves was the best decision we ever made. We would never have escaped the rat race without it.
And once our investment train was rattling full steam ahead, the amount we saved made a big difference in how quickly we reached our financial destination.
The trick to saving more of your money is knowing where to start.
Many people I know fling their hands up in despair at the wall of challenges:
Chuck in a seemingly permanent cost-of-living crisis, and it can feel impossible to even begin to chip away at this list. Especially on a normal income.
Yet every journey begins with a single step. And, in my case, a website.
To fix the bad habits of a lifetime you need a helping hand. Personally I found it at MoneySavingExpert.
I’d like to say it was a book that changed my life, but really it was this website.
You know it already. The site’s founder, Martin Lewis, has become ubiquitous as a financial TV evangelist: preaching and teaching Britons how to save cash.
But even in today’s world of savings apps, neo-banks with built-in budgeting tools, and enough financial influencers to fill Wembley Stadium, the original might still be the best.

That’s because MoneySavingExpert (or MSE to its friends) is at its most potent when it’s exploited as a programme to turn around your finances. Used like this, it can help you map the way forward with the inspiration, knowledge, and the tools you need to dramatically change your spending habits – rather than just doing the work for you.
Teach a man to fish, and all that. 1
The first move has to be yours, of course. For my part, I needed to admit that the way I was running my financial affairs – or ignoring them – was a problem.
But after that Mrs Accumulator and I turned to MSE to do something about it.
Where was all our money going? We thought we knew, but the truth was our bank account had more leaks than the government before Budget Day.
The spending scales only really fall from your eyes when you’re forced to account for everything. Yes, everything – from your early morning Starbucks to your summer holidays.
That sounds like ten shades of agony until you discover the hard graft has been done for you by MoneySavingExpert’s Budget Planner. (Scroll down a bit after clicking through).
This fantastic tool rounds up every relevant expense in an easy-to-swallow online form. All you’ve got to do is fill in the numbers to see the state you’re in.
Once you know where the money goes, you can work out how to stem the flow.
Yep, this is self-evidently crucial. We all pay so many bills it’s like we’ve got financial fleas.

But if we can cut the blood-suckers down to size then there will be a bit more cash left at the end of every month to have some fun with. (Like sticking it away for 20 years in a low-cost tracker fund. That’s my kind of fun!)
However, while it may be obvious, few of us find the time to get a good deal. Or we sort out the gas and electricity but forget about squeezing insurance premiums or motoring costs.
Again, MoneySavingExpert charges to the rescue. The site’s easy-to-follow guides show you how to score a great deal without wasting your life.
Go to the full Money Makeover page. Here are all life’s expenses lined up like ducks in a row. Shoot them all down. One by one. Large and small.
Martin Lewis reckons the average person gains the equivalent of a 25% pay-rise by completing the makeover.
I don’t know exactly how much we saved, but it was easily into hundreds of pounds a year.
Here’s the key question Mrs Accumulator and I had to ask ourselves:
What do you really enjoy in life?
The answer more than doubled the amount we could save.
With our spending habits laid bare by the Budget Planner, we could go down the list and cross out the things we didn’t really need / want / think were worth the money.
Personal finance articles invariably home in on a go-to list of potentially wasteful expenditures, including:
In fact, anything you buy on autopilot should be scrutinised and struck off, or substituted for a cheaper alternative.
For example, perhaps you haven’t watched anything on Disney Plus since binging on Marvel six months ago. Cancel it.
You do use your gym membership, but would a no-frills operation do the trick?

Cognitive dissonance corner: Naturally you should never apply this kind of thinking to Monevator ​membership​. That’s sacrosanct. Sign-up today if you’ve not done so already. Cut down by a pint a month instead, and both your bank account and your waistline will thank you!
Here are a couple of mental tricks to assist your austerity drive:
This is a shock tactic designed to stop you spending. The tool reveals the annual outlay on any particular item and how long you must work to afford it.
It turns out I was spending £200 a year on a weekly bacon sandwich 2. I could twiddle my thumbs over an even bigger wodge of a global tracker fund if I invested that instead.
Buy a shirt for £60 and it actually costs the average Joe about £83 in earnings, before tax. 3
That shirt was an expensive luxury at £60, but now I realise I’ve got to earn £83 to pay for it, I can’t put it back on the rack quickly enough.
The idea isn’t to make yourself miserable every time you spend a penny. Rather, it’s to make yourself think twice about what’s really worth spending money on.
The Demotivator tool helps you visualise whether seemingly harmless expenses are worth their long-term cost.

The before-tax price tag helps you to resist the allure of impulse purchases. If adding almost 50% to the price of an item helps you see how hard you’re working to pay for it, then you can assess its true worth to you, even in the heat of consumption arousal.

It’s easy to get embarrassed about thrifty living and to write yourself off as an old skinflint. But the emotional pay-off from controlling your spending is every bit as great as the financial benefits of saving more.
We know we can’t afford everything we want. Trying to have it all is a shortcut to anxiety and possible disaster.
But by figuring out what we really value in life, we can spend more time doing the things that make us happy while saving enough to secure our future financial well-being.
Though perhaps the fisherman’s union would have something to say about it.
Approximately, assuming basic-rate income tax @ 20%, National Insurance @8%, and not worrying about personal allowances, thresholds, or the odd penny.
